newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN hopes to fly home Rwandan refugees from Zaire.
newsitem.headline: UN hopes to fly home Rwandan refugees from Zaire.

text.p: The United Nations refugee agency is negotiating with Zaire to begin flying home the most vulnerable refugees among more than 200,000 Rwandans still in the country, a senior official said on Thursday.
These include families headed by women, unaccompanied minors and those too frail to walk or ride trucks once land repatriation becomes possible.

Sergio Vieira de Mello, assistant High Commissioner for Refugees, also said the agency hoped Tanzania would allow thousands of Rwandan refugees to be screened to determine whether they want to go home or seek asylum.
But Vieira de Mello told a news briefing there was no question of forcing people back to Burundi after last week's massacre by troops of 122 Hutus expelled from Tanzania.
"Returning to Burundi is exposing people to danger. Returning them to Rwanda, we believe, does not expose them to danger except for those who have blood on their hands," he said.
"A number of international staff have come to the conclusion that the majority (in Zaire)...are indeed willing to return if they are given that possibility," Vieira de Mello said.

"The main problem is clearance from the Zairean government and clearance from the Rwandan government. Rwanda has said "yes', and we are negotiating right now -- in fact we began yesterday negotiating with the Zairean government," he added.

The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) is trying to bring life-saving aid to 120,000 refugees near the remote Zaire village of Tingi-Tingi, who fled there after fighting broke out between Rwandan-backed rebels and Zairean troops in October.
U.N. officials said at least 255 people had died in Tingi-Tingi, south of Lubutu town, between January 3-14.
Another 40,000 are north in Amisi, while at least 70,000 Rwandan and Burundis refugees are scattered in an inaccessible area around Shabunda, some 160 kms (100 miles) west of Bukavu.
Repatriation by air is not routine, but UNHCR has done it in Africa since the 1970s in cases where travel over land is nearly impossible due to fighting, according to the Brazilian.

"What we are trying to do right now is to ascertain whether we can charter civilian aircraft, Antonov-21 type of aircraft, not too heavy for those airstrips which are generally in bad condition, but not too small so as to be able to transport a meaningful number of people," Vieira de Mello said.
UNHCR hoped to get permission from the Zairean government to move the refugees from Shabunda west to Kalima, which has a proper landing strip where more aid could be transported.
"We would then try to fly vulnerable ones back until such time as we can actually open a land corridor," he said.
Rebel advances in the east uprooted more than a million Hutu refugees who had fled to Zaire after civil war and massacre of up to a million Tutsis in Rwanda in 1994 by Hutu hardliners.
Some 700,000 have gone home, according to UNHCR. But many headed deeper into Zaire, fearing persecution if they returned to Rwanda, now ruled by a mainly Tutsi government.
